name: Start a fire with a bow drill
blurb: The hardest fire skill worth learning and the most satisfying. Success depends almost entirely on materials and geometry — when it fails it is nearly always dry-enough wood, not weak arms.
gear: Dry softwood for spindle and hearth board: willow, cedar, cottonwood, lime
A curved green branch and a bootlace for the bow
A hardwood or stone bearing block
A tinder bundle of dry grass, bark fibre or cattail fluff
steps: Choose the wood: spindle and hearth board should be the same dry softwood, light enough to dent with a thumbnail but not rotten.
Carve a spindle about 20 cm long and thumb-thick, pointed at the top and blunter at the bottom, and cut a shallow socket in the hearth board near the edge.
Burn in the socket first — run the drill until you have a black, matched depression — then cut a precise pie-slice notch, one-eighth of the circle, to collect the dust.
Set your body: left foot on the board, left wrist locked against your shin, bearing block held down hard and straight. Rigid geometry is more important than speed.
Bow long, smooth, full strokes to build black dust in the notch, then go faster and heavier for a final burst until smoke rises from the dust pile itself.
Let the ember sit for 20 seconds, transfer it to your tinder bundle, and blow steadily from underneath until it flames.
tips: Smoke is not an ember. Everything smokes; only a self-sustaining coal in the notch matters.
Wobble kills it. If the spindle jumps out, your bearing hand is not locked against your leg.
Prepare the tinder bundle and all your kindling before you take the first stroke.
proof: You produce an ember and blow it into flame, twice, using materials you gathered yourself.
